chunks: Al-Mudhaffar ibn Ja'far al-Alawi al-Samarqandi narrated that Ja'far ibn Mas'ood, from his father Abi al-Nasr Muhammad ibn Mas'ood al-Ayyashi, from Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal, from Muhammad ibn al-Walid, from al-Abbas ibn Hilal, from Ali ibn Musa al-Rida (peace be upon him), from his father Musa, from his father Ja'far, from his father Muhammad, from his father Ali ibn al-Husayn, from his father al-Husayn ibn Ali, from his father Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him) who said:

The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Five things I will not abandon until death: eating while sitting on the ground with the slaves, riding my donkey with a saddle, milking the goat with my own hand, wearing wool, and greeting the children, so that they become a tradition after me.'

key_terms.التَّسْلِيمُ: Greeting (specifically saying 'As-salamu alaykum'), highlighting the Prophet's initiative in greeting even children to normalize the practice.
key_terms.الصُّوفُ: Wool, referring to simple, coarse clothing worn by the Prophet as a sign of humility and detachment from luxury.
key_terms.الْحَضِيضُ: The ground or floor, indicating eating while seated directly on it rather than on raised furniture or beds.
key_terms.سُنَّةٌ: Tradition or established practice, indicating that these actions were intended to become normative behaviors for the Muslim community.
key_terms.مُؤْكَفًا: Equipped with a saddle or pack saddle, indicating the use of a simple, functional saddle for the donkey.

ai.seo_question: What are the five practices the Prophet Muhammad said he would not abandon until death?
ai.summary: Transmitted through the pristine chain of the Twelve Imams in Shaykh al-Saduq’s *‘Uyun Akhbar al-Rida*, this hadith highlights the Prophet’s deliberate adoption of humble, everyday practices to counter aristocratic pretensions and establish a model of accessible leadership. These five acts—eating with servants, riding a tethered donkey, milking goats, wearing wool, and greeting children—serve as enduring *sunnah* that emphasize social equality, manual labor, and approachability, reinforcing the Shia emphasis on the Prophet’s human simplicity alongside his divine status.
